Subject: Get Started with a Professional Mix on a Budget

Dear [Recipient's Name],

I'd like to introduce you to our "Starter Mix" service, designed specifically for DIY musicians on a tight budget. For a flat fee, you'll receive a high-quality mix of one track, including:

* A stock-plus-analog-modeled pass to give your track a professional sheen
* One revision to ensure you're completely satisfied
* A stereo bounce ready for distribution

Our typical turnaround time is about five days, so you can get back to focusing on your music without delay.

To help you take your mix to the next level, we'll include a 10-minute mentoring note detailing workflow changes you can make next time around. This will give you valuable insights to improve your mixing skills and achieve even better results in the future.

If you're not quite ready for a full mix, or you'd like to get a feel for our mixing style, we're happy to offer a free 10-minute critique. Simply send over a rough stem pack and we'll provide you with actionable feedback to help you improve your mix.

Choose between our "Starter Mix" service or send us a rough stem pack for a free critique. Either way, we're here to help

task_instruction: Encouraging critique about emotional delivery with technical suggestions
task_details: Song verse needs more vulnerability; performance sounded technically fine but emotionally distant. Provide vocal delivery techniques (breathiness, dynamic range), mic proximity, mixing cues (reverb type and settings) to enhance intimacy.
personalized: I hear the right phrasing, but the verse could use more vulnerability—it feels a touch guarded. Try a breathy, lower-intensity delivery on the next pass, sing closer to the mic for warmth and lower your volume by 3–5 dB to pull listeners in. task_instruction: Dynamics control critique and suggested compressor settings
task_details: Recorded DI and vocal through 1073. Issue: wildly inconsistent dynamics, some peaks clipping the preamp. Advise on tracking compression settings to use next time and mixing compression chain (hardware vs plugin) with target gain reduction values.
personalized: You're riding big dynamics and it's spiking the pre. On tracking use a gentle compressor with a 3:1 ratio, attack around 10 ms and release ~100 ms, aim for 4–6 dB of gain reduction on the loudest peaks. If you prefer a hardware chain try the LA-2A for smoothing or a 1176 with medium attack for more snap. In the mix I'll use parallel compression to bring body without killing the transients; set the wet bus with about +4 dB drive and ride the fader for emotion. Also back off the input gain so peaks never exceed -6 dBFS to leave headroom for saturation.
prompt:
Write a email

- Problem to address: riding big dynamics is spiking the preamp.
- Tracking instructions: use a gentle compressor with 3:1 ratio, attack ~10 ms, release ~100 ms; target ~4–6 dB of gain reduction on the loudest peaks.
- Hardware alternatives for tracking: LA-2A for smoothing; 1176 with medium attack for more snap.
- Mixing approach: use parallel compression to add body without killing transients; set the wet bus with about +4 dB drive; ride the fader to shape emotional dynamics.

Subject: Tracking and Mixing Guidance for Big Dynamics

Dear [Name],

I hope this email finds you well. I wanted to follow up on the tracking and mixing approach for the big dynamics. 

In terms of tracking, I recommend using a gentle compressor with a 3:1 ratio, attack time of approximately 10 ms, and release time of about 100 ms. This should allow you to target around 4-6 dB of gain reduction on the loudest peaks without over-compressing the signal.

For hardware alternatives, you can consider using the LA-2A for a smoother sound or the 1176 with a medium attack time for a more dynamic sound.

When it comes to mixing, I suggest using parallel compression to add body to the sound without sacrificing the transients. To do this, set the wet bus with around +4 dB of drive and ride the fader to shape the emotional dynamics of the track.

In terms of gain staging, please reduce the input gain so that the peaks never exceed -6 dBFS, leaving headroom for saturation and optimal processing.

If you have any questions or need further clarification on any of these points, please don't hesitate to reach out.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

[Your Name]

Subject: Vinyl Mastering Services for Your Upcoming 12-inch Release

Dear [Recipient's Name],

I hope this email finds you well. I came across your project and noticed you're planning a 12-inch vinyl release. I'd like to offer my vinyl-specific mastering services to help ensure your music sounds its best on this format.

Our mastering process focuses on enhancing the low-end by summing it to mono below approximately 150 Hz, controlling excessive sibilance and stereo width to create a balanced sound, and advising on side length to preserve the punch and energy of your tracks. This attention to detail will help your music translate well on vinyl.

Deliverables will include a test cut file for your review and a premaster ready for the lacquer, ensuring a smooth production process.

Typically, our turnaround time is one week, but I'd like to schedule a 20-minute call with you to finalize the track order and spacing between songs. This will allow us to ensure the optimal flow and pacing of your release. Would you be available for a call at your convenience to discuss the details?

Please let me know if you're interested, and we can schedule a time that works for you.

Best regards,

[Your Name]

task_instruction: Recommend low-cut/HF settings for non-vocal tracks to reduce build-up.
task_details: Client notes muddiness and mud layering across mix. Propose HPF frequencies for common tracks (guitars, keys, percussion), with slope recommendations and a note on exceptions.
personalized: General clean-up: high-pass non-vocal tracks aggressively but musically. Rhythm guitars and synth pads: HPF at 100–140 Hz, drums (overheads) HPF at 200–250 Hz to reduce low rumble, percussion/shakers HPF at 500–700 Hz if they're clashy, and keyboards that sit in top end HPF at 120–150 Hz. Use 12 dB/oct or 18 dB/oct slopes to keep things natural. Exceptions: Kick and bass should remain full. For acoustic instruments that need body, back off to 80–100 Hz. These cuts free up headroom and reduce mud without thinning the arrangement.
prompt:
Write a email

- Purpose: Request a general clean-up of the mix by applying high-pass filtering to non-vocal tracks to free up headroom and reduce mud while keeping the arrangement full and natural.
- Apply HPF to these track types with these ranges:
  - Rhythm guitars and synth pads: 100–140 Hz.
  - Drums (overheads): 200–250 Hz (to reduce low rumble).
  - Percussion/shakers (if they are clashy): 500–700 Hz.
  - Keyboards that sit in the top end: 120–150 Hz.
- Use filter slopes of 12 dB/oct or 18 dB/oct.
- Exceptions/adjustments:
  - Do not remove low-end weight from kick and bass; keep them full.
  - For acoustic instruments that need body, reduce HPF to 80–100 Hz.
  - Apply higher HPF on percussion/shakers only when they are clashy.
- Intended outcome: These cuts should free up headroom and reduce mud without thinning the arrangement.

task_instruction: Explain proper gain-staging for a rock tracking session
task_details: Session: four-piece alt-metal band tracked live with overdubs. You had DI guitar, two SM57s on guitar cabs, Neumann on vocals, room mics, drum kit with overheads and kick in. Goal: teach the junior engineer how to set clean gain structure from tracking into Pro Tools for future mixing, include concrete dB targets and routing advice. Mention headroom numbers, clipping avoidance, analog preamp gain hints, and saving a reference screenshot or note.
personalized:
Hey — quick note on gain-staging for the session we did last night. Start with a clean gain stage at the console or preamp: aim for an average of -18 dBFS on your meters with peaks around -6 dBFS on the loudest hits, so we leave headroom for summing and plugins later. For drums, get the kick and snare peaks to sit near -6 dBFS, overheads around -12 to -10 dBFS, room mics a little lower. Guitar cabs with SM57s should clip the preamps on the hot bits long before the DAW destroys anything, so set preamp gain until the analog LED occasionally kisses yellow, then back a hair so Pro Tools sits around -18 peak average. For the Neumann vocal, set gain so the loudest shout or belted line peaks around -6 dBFS while normal phrases sit near -18. If someone’s riding dynamics, use light compression or ask for consistent distance rather than slam the preamp.

Route tracks clean: send direct inputs into labeled tracks, buss overheads to a stereo overhead bus and rooms to a separate bus so we can treat them without touching individual channels. Turn off any channel inserts that introduce latency while tracking, and disable automatic plugin compensation. Save a short snapshot: screenshot your input gain settings or write them in the session notes, include preamp model and trim setting. If you hit red on the DAW, pull gain at the preamp first, never defang the mic with a limiter unless it's an emergency.

Yeah, rough, but stick to those numbers and we'll avoid digital clipping and keep good headroom for editing and saturation later. Save the session as trackgain_v1 and mark which tracks were hot so mixing knows where to start.

- Define routing and session-organization requirements to simplify later mixing.
- Instruct what to save in session notes and how to respond if the DAW clips.

- General headroom target: aim for an average of -18 dBFS on meters with peaks around -6 dBFS on the loudest hits to leave headroom for summing and plugins.
- Drums: kick and snare peaks near -6 dBFS; overheads around -12 to -10 dBFS; room mics a bit lower than overheads.
- Guitar cabs (SM57): set preamp gain so analog preamp LED occasionally reaches yellow on the hot bits, then back slightly so the DAW averages around -18 dBFS (analog may clip before DAW).

task_instruction: Fix a monitor wedge that's not loud enough for the drummer.
task_details: Drummer complains that their wedge on aux 3 is too quiet even with fader up. Monitor sends appear to be working for other wedges. Console is digital with pre/post options. The drummer needs a louder click and kick in-ear alternative not available. Provide quick checks and settings to restore sufficient level without clipping FOH or damaging ears.
personalized: Alright, get the drummer what they need without frying anything. First confirm aux 3 is set to post-fader on the console; if it’s pre, they won't hear mix changes. Trim channel sends from the kick and click to aux 3 and set the send trims so the loudest hits sit around -12 dBFS into the monitor bus. Increase the master of aux 3 gradually but keep headroom; don't push it above +6 dBu on the amp. If you're driving a passive wedge, check the amp gain and speaker wiring—raise amp output but keep amplifier clip LED off. If wedges are overloaded, split the monitor between wedge and a small stage amp and send click + kick to the amp only. Finally, add a gentle 80 Hz high-pass at 60–80 Hz on the wedge to prevent rumble and a 3–6 dB boost at 3–5 kHz for click definition. Tell the drummer to cup their ear and give feedback so we can fine-tune.

- Increase the master level of Aux 3 gradually while keeping headroom; do not drive the amp above +6 dBu.

Please ensure that Aux 3 on the console is set to post-fader, as this will allow the drummer to hear mix changes.

Subject: Thinning a Guitar DI Signal

Dear [Recipient],

I wanted to share with you a few methods to thicken a guitar DI signal. The primary approach is to re-amp the DI through a tube amp or use amp simulations to add warmth and depth to your sound.

**Re-amping with a Real Amp:**

1. Set the amp to a clean to lightly overdriven setting.
2. Set the EQ flat, with the presence around 4-5 and the bass around 4. Slightly boost the mids to around 6 to maintain the guitar's cut.
3. Place a Shure SM57 about 2-3 inches off-center of the speaker cone to capture the amp's tone.
4. Additionally, place a ribbon or condenser mic 8-12 inches back to capture the room's ambiance.

**Amp Simulation Approach:**

1. Use a combination of amp simulations, stacking a tight "British"-style amp (for mid bump) with an American-style amp behind it (for sheen).
2. Choose a cabinet IR with a small room impulse to add depth and space to your sound.

**Level Guidelines:**

When re-amping, keep the re-amped signal around -10 to -6 dB

Regards,
Marcus Hale

Subject: Final Pass Checklist for Mastering

Dear [Engineer's Name],

I've compiled the final pass checklist for mastering. Please review and confirm that the following items are satisfactory:

- Master bus level: peaks must not exceed -6 dB FS.
- Master bus RMS target: approximately -14 to -12 dB (appropriate for the genre).
- Mono-check: 
  - Verify no phase cancellation issues.
  - Special attention to drums and background vocals (BGs) to ensure no loss of energy.
- Low-end check: 
  - Kick fundamental focused between 60–80 Hz.
  - Remove unnecessary energy below 40 Hz.
- High-frequency check: 
  - Address any buildup above 8–10 kHz.
  - Apply a gentle shelf if necessary to reduce harshness.
- Vocal intelligibility: 
  - Lead vocal should sit +1–2 dB above the background vocals in choruses.
  - Ensure clear readability on headphones.
- Noise/click removal: 
  - Remove audible clicks/pops.
  - Denoise so the noise floor is consistent.

If all items are green, please bounce the stems as previously outlined.

task_instruction: Explain dealing with latency and plugin delay compensation during tracking
task_details: Junior engineer tracking with low-latency needs. Describe how to minimize monitor latency, recommend which plugins to avoid in monitor paths, explain using direct monitoring, and steps to check for sample/latency misalignment post-recording.
personalized:
Latency drill: tracking requires <10 ms to feel natural. Use direct monitoring on the interface when possible and disable high-latency plugins on the monitor path. If you must use plugins for tone, use low-latency modes or hardware like an analog preamp and re-amp later. In Pro Tools, enable delay compensation but be mindful that some insert chains will add latency.

After recording, check alignment by recording a short test and zooming into the transient; if it's shifted, use delay compensation or nudge recorded regions to correct it. Note which tracks used latency-inducing plugins so mixing knows to render or freeze them. If the singer complains about delay, switch to direct monitoring and route headphone mix through a low-latency path immediately.
prompt:
Write a email that conveys the following key objectives and factual information:

- Goal: Ensure performer monitoring latency stays below 10 ms so monitoring feels natural.
- Primary monitoring recommendation: Use direct monitoring on the interface when possible.
- Preventive action: Disable high‑latency plugins on the monitor/headphone path.
- If plugins are needed for tone: use low‑latency plugin modes when available, or use an analog preamp during tracking and re‑amp/process later.
- Pro Tools note: Enable Delay Compensation, but be aware some insert chains will still add latency.
- Post‑recording alignment check: Record a short test take and zoom into the transient to verify timing; if the recorded transient is shifted, correct by using delay compensation or nudging recorded regions.
- Documentation: Note which tracks used latency‑inducing plugins so mixing can render or freeze those tracks.
- Immediate troubleshooting: If the singer complains about delay, switch them to direct monitoring and route their headphone mix through a low‑latency path immediately.
style_agnostic:
Subject: Optimizing Performer Monitoring Latency

Dear [Recipient's Name],

To ensure a natural monitoring experience for our performers, it is crucial that we maintain a monitoring latency of 10 ms or less. To achieve this goal, we recommend the following best practices:

When possible, we suggest using direct monitoring on the interface. However, if plugins are required for tone, please disable high-latency plugins on the monitor/headphone path to prevent excessive delay.

If low-latency plugin modes are available, please utilize them. Alternatively, consider using an analog preamp during tracking and re-amp/process later to minimize latency.

In Pro Tools, enable Delay Compensation to account for latency. Nevertheless, be aware that some insert chains will still introduce latency. To verify timing, record a short test take and zoom into the transient to check for any shifts. If necessary, correct the timing using delay compensation or nudging recorded regions.

For documentation purposes, please note which tracks utilize latency-inducing plugins, so mixing can render or freeze those tracks accordingly.

In the event of an immediate issue, if the singer complains about delay, switch them to direct monitoring and route their headphone mix through a low-latency path immediately.

Thank you for your attention to this matter, and please let me know

If bass collapses, check low-end stereo imaging and use a high-pass on sides below 120 Hz or fold low frequencies to mono with an MS EQ.

Make a mono-friendly mix first and then expand stereo elements, ride the fader in chorus sections to keep energy. We'll do a final mono check before exporting so the track translates to clubs and radios.

Dear [Recipient's Name],

I hope this email finds you well. I am writing to confirm the cutting parameters for the upcoming lacquer cuts. As per our previous discussions, I have outlined the key specifications below for your review and approval.

- Cutting Format: Stereo
- Average Peak Headroom: -3 dB
- Low-Frequency Handling: Mono-sum below 60 Hz
- LF Roll-in: 45 Hz roll-in at -6 dB/oct (to protect the inner groove)
- Modulation Limits: Keep under 8 dB

To ensure timely scheduling with the lacquer house, I kindly request that you review and confirm these parameters by this Friday at 2:00 PM CST. If you are unable to confirm these parameters, please provide alternate target levels immediately so we can proceed with scheduling the cut for Monday.

Additionally, please note that the master file specifications are as follows: 24-bit, 48 kHz WAV, normalized to -0.3 dB FS.

Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter. I look forward to hearing back from you by the specified deadline.

Best regards,
[Your Name]
Cutting Engineer

Dear [Recipient],

I appreciate you considering me for the job, but I'm currently booked and unavailable to take it on right now. Unfortunately, this means I won't be able to deliver a midnight-ready mix tonight as originally requested.

I want to emphasize that I prefer not to deliver rushed work or a product that hasn't had a proper revision pass. I believe this not only ensures a higher quality outcome but also allows for a more sustainable workflow.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

task_instruction: Guide on automating mix rides for choruses and dynamic sections

personalized:
Automation basics: ride the fader on the chorus to make the vocal sit on top, start with +1.5 to +3 dB boosts on the lead vocal for the chorus and automate back for verses. Use write or touch mode in Pro Tools and play the section while adjusting faders, then clean up the automation in the lanes. For guitars, automate slightly down in verse to leave room for the vocal and open up in the bridge.

Prefer volume rides for musical balance and reserve heavy compression for control, not constant push. Automate send levels for reverb and delay to bring ambience up on big phrases and duck it on intimate lines. Name automation passes like ChorusRide_v1 so we don't overwrite. Keep changes musical and subtle; if it feels like a spotlight, you're close.

Dear [Recipient's Name],

To make the lead vocal sit on top of the mix, I recommend riding the fader on the chorus to allow the vocal to sit on top. To achieve this, I suggest starting with a +1.5 to +3 dB boost on the lead vocal during the chorus and automating it back down for the verses. task_instruction: Coach on checking and correcting phase issues across multiple mics
task_details: Drums and guitar cabinets tracked with multiple mics show phase problems. Teach how to detect phase cancellation, use polarity invert and delay compensation, and document corrections in session notes. Include a practical workflow and mention tools like the phase meter or mono-sum checks.
personalized:
Phase troubleshooting workflow: first, sum to mono and listen for thin highs or weak low end — that's our tell. Solo the suspect mics, flip the polarity on one and listen for the biggest improvement; if it thickens up, keep the polarity flipped. If polarity flip doesn't fix it, nudge the region timing by small ms increments or use short plugin delay compensation to align transients. For drums, align kick to close mics and snare top to snare bottom by zooming into the transient and moving samples until peaks match.

Use a phase meter or correlation meter to confirm; aim for positive correlation without being fully mono. Document any timing shifts in the session notes with ms values and which tracks were adjusted so mix can recall. If you're routing multiple close mics to a sub-bus, check phase in the bus context; sometimes two mics sound fine solo but cancel in the bus. Save a session labeled phasefixed_v1 after you finish.
prompt:
Write a email

- Purpose: identify and fix phase issues in a multitrack session so the mix retains low end and clarity.

- Diagnostic tell: sum the session to mono and listen for thin highs or weak low end.

- Initial fix: solo the suspect microphones and flip the polarity (invert) on one mic; if the sound thickens, keep the polarity flipped.

- If polarity flip fails: nudge the timing of the region by small millisecond increments or apply a short plugin delay compensation to align transients.

- Drum-specific alignment: align kick to close mics; align snare top to snare bottom by zooming into the transient and moving samples until peaks match.

- Measurement/verification: use a phase meter or correlation meter and aim for positive correlation without making the mix fully mono.

- Bus-check: when routing multiple close mics to a sub-bus, check phase in the bus context because pairs that sound fine solo can cancel when summed.

- Documentation: record any timing shifts in the session notes, including the ms values and which tracks were adjusted so the mix can be recalled.

- File naming: save the finished session as phasefixed_v1.

task_instruction: Advise on mixing strategies to keep vocals sitting above heavy guitar mixes
task_details: Mix challenge: dense guitar wall threatens to mask the vocal. Provide EQ, compression, automation, and arrangement suggestions, including frequency ranges to cut/boost and bus processing tips to make vocals cut through without over-brightening.
personalized:
Getting vocals to cut: carve guitars around the vocal's main frequencies. If the vocal sits around 1.5–3 kHz, notch guitars between 1–3 kHz with broad Q cuts of 2–3 dB. Add a touch of presence to the vocal with a narrow boost around 3–5 kHz and open up air above 10 kHz if needed. Use parallel compression on vocals to raise body without pushing sibilance; send to a compressed aux and blend in.

Automation is key: ride the vocal fader on choruses and bridge and automate guitar bus levels down slightly during important lines. Use mid-side processing to keep guitars wider and vocals in the center. For the guitar bus, consider a mild bus compression and stereo width reduction at low frequencies so the vocal has room. Keep it aggressive but singable—if it still gets lost, carve more out of the guitars and we’ll preserve the mix energy.
prompt:
Write a email

- Purpose: Instruct a mixing engineer on techniques to make the lead vocal cut through the guitars.
- Vocal target range: vocal sits around 1.5–3 kHz (use this as reference).
- Guitar EQ action: notch guitars between 1–3 kHz with broad Q cuts of about 2–3 dB to create space for the vocal.
- Vocal EQ action: add a narrow boost around 3–5 kHz for presence; open up air above 10 kHz if needed.
- Compression: use parallel compression on vocals — send the vocal to a compressed aux and blend that return to raise body without increasing sibilance.
- Automation: ride the vocal fader on choruses and the bridge; automate guitar bus levels down slightly during important vocal lines.
- Stereo imaging: use mid-side processing to keep guitars wider and vocals centered.
- Guitar bus processing: apply mild bus compression and reduce stereo width at low frequencies so the vocal has room.
- Balancing guideline: keep the overall sound aggressive but singable; if the vocal is still getting lost, carve more out of the guitars while preserving mix energy.

task_instruction: Addressing sibilance and de-essing strategy
task_details: Section: bridge contains harsh sibilants. Provide immediate corrective actions (mic angle/placement), de-esser plugin settings (frequency, threshold), and editorial advice (consonant pulls), plus how to avoid artifacts.
personalized: Bridge has harsh sibilants that cut through in a jagged way. First, move a hair off-axis or angle the mic to reduce energy at 6–10 kHz. For the mix try a de-esser tuned to 6.5–8 kHz with a threshold around -18 dB and ~4–6 dB of gain reduction when it hits, or use split-band de-essing to preserve tonal body. Editorially, pull consonants slightly back in the comp if they smack the line, and don't overdo the de-esser or you'll turn the voice dull. Those steps will keep the consonants clean without stripping presence.

Write a email

- Mix adjustment: apply a de-esser tuned to approximately 6.5–8 kHz.
- De-esser settings: threshold around -18 dB; aim for roughly 4–6 dB of gain reduction when the de-esser engages.
- Alternative processing: consider split-band de-essing to control sibilance while preserving tonal body.
- Editorial adjustment: pull problematic consonants slightly back in the comp if they "smack the line."
- Constraint/caution: avoid overdoing the de-esser (risk of making the voice dull).
- Desired outcome: consonants are clean and controlled without stripping presence.

I wanted to discuss the vocal track labeled "Bridge" as it has harsh, jagged sibilants that cut through the mix. To reduce this harshness while preserving the vocal presence and tonal body, I recommend the following adjustments:

To start, let's try making some recording adjustments. Please move the microphone a hair off-axis or angle it to reduce energy in the 6–10 kHz range. This should help minimize the sibilant issues without affecting the overall sound.
